disclaimer: These tools provide general emotional wellness support and are not medical treatments.

grounding.name: Grounding Techniques
grounding.description: Evidence-based sensory exercises to anchor you in the present moment, reducing anxiety and dissociation.

exercises.name: 5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Grounding
steps: Notice 5 things you can SEE around you right now.
Notice 4 things you can TOUCH — feel their texture.
Notice 3 things you can HEAR in your environment.
Notice 2 things you can SMELL (or two scents you like).
Notice 1 thing you can TASTE.
exercises.tip: Speak each item aloud if you can — the act of naming helps ground you further.

exercises.name: Safe Place Visualization
steps: Close your eyes and take three slow breaths.
Picture a place — real or imagined — where you feel completely safe and at peace.
Notice details: colors, sounds, the temperature of the air.
Allow yourself to stay there for a few moments.
Slowly return to the room, carrying that sense of calm.
exercises.tip: You can return to this place any time you feel unsafe or overwhelmed.

breathing.name: Breathing Exercises
breathing.description: Controlled breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing physiological stress response.

exercises.name: Box Breathing (4-4-4-4)
steps: Breathe IN slowly for 4 counts.
HOLD your breath for 4 counts.
Breathe OUT slowly for 4 counts.
HOLD again for 4 counts.
Repeat 4–6 times.
exercises.tip: Used by Navy SEALs and athletes to achieve calm focus under pressure.

exercises.name: 4-7-8 Calming Breath
steps: Exhale completely through your mouth.
Close your mouth and inhale quietly through your nose for 4 counts.
Hold your breath for 7 counts.
Exhale completely through your mouth for 8 counts.
Repeat this cycle 3–4 times.
exercises.tip: Works especially well before sleep or when anxiety spikes suddenly.

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic (Belly) Breathing
steps: Place one hand on your chest, one on your belly.
Breathe in through your nose — your belly should rise, chest stays still.
Exhale through pursed lips, belly falls.
Repeat slowly for 5–10 breaths.
exercises.tip: This is the body's natural calming breath. Practice daily for lasting results.

cbt_reframing.name: CBT-Style Cognitive Reframing
cbt_reframing.description: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy-inspired exercises to identify and gently challenge unhelpful thought patterns.
cbt_reframing.disclaimer: These are self-help tools, not therapy. A licensed therapist provides personalized CBT treatment.

exercises.name: Thought Record
steps: Write down the situation triggering distress.
Write the automatic thought: what did your mind say?
Rate how strongly you believe it (0–100%).
List evidence that SUPPORTS the thought.
List evidence that CONTRADICTS the thought.
Write a more balanced alternative thought.
Rate how strongly you believe the original thought now.
exercises.tip: Often, writing it out reveals thoughts are more extreme than reality supports.

exercises.name: The Friend Test
steps: Think about what you're being hard on yourself about.
Imagine your closest friend was in the exact same situation.
What would you say to them — with compassion?
Now say exactly that to yourself.
exercises.tip: We are often far kinder to others than to ourselves. You deserve that same compassion.

exercises.name: Decatastrophizing
steps: Identify the feared outcome: 'What am I afraid will happen?'
Ask: How likely is this outcome, really? What is the evidence?
Ask: If it does happen, what is the worst realistic outcome?
Ask: Could I cope with that? What resources do I have?
Ask: What is the BEST possible outcome? What is most LIKELY?
exercises.tip: Catastrophizing amplifies fear. Reality-testing shrinks it back to size.

journaling.name: Guided Journaling Prompts
journaling.description: Structured writing exercises to process emotions, gain perspective, and build self-awareness.

exercises.name: Emotion Dump
exercises.prompt: Set a timer for 10 minutes. Write everything you're feeling right now — no filter, no judgment. No one will read this. Just let it out on the page.

exercises.name: Three Good Things
exercises.prompt: Write down three things that went okay today — they don't have to be big. One sentence for each. What made each one happen?

exercises.name: Letter to Your Future Self
exercises.prompt: Write a short letter to yourself 6 months from now. What do you hope has changed? What strength are you beginning to discover? Seal it (digitally or physically) and set a reminder to read it.

exercises.name: Self-Compassion Letter
exercises.prompt: Think of a situation causing you suffering. Write a letter to yourself from the perspective of a deeply compassionate friend — one who knows your struggles and wishes only kindness for you.

stress_management.name: Stress Management Techniques
stress_management.description: Practical, evidence-backed techniques for managing acute and chronic stress.

exercises.name: Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR)
steps: Find a comfortable seated or lying position.
Starting with your feet: tense the muscles tightly for 5 seconds.
Release suddenly and feel the relaxation spread for 30 seconds.
Move up: calves → thighs → abdomen → hands → arms → shoulders → face.
After completing the sequence, breathe slowly and enjoy the calm.
exercises.tip: PMR has strong clinical evidence for reducing anxiety and improving sleep.

exercises.name: Mindful Walk
steps: Step outside (even just around the block).
Leave your phone in your pocket.
Focus entirely on your senses as you walk.
Notice the ground under each step, the air on your skin, sounds around you.
If your mind wanders, gently return attention to your steps.
exercises.tip: Physical movement + fresh air + mindfulness is a powerful stress-relief combination.

exercises.name: Worry Time (Time-Boxing Anxiety)
steps: Set a specific 15-minute 'worry time' each day (e.g., 5pm).
When anxious thoughts arise earlier, note them briefly and tell yourself: 'I'll address this at worry time.'
During worry time, freely think through your concerns.
When the timer ends, consciously close the session.
Gradually, your brain learns that worrying has a container.
exercises.tip: This technique separates worry from other parts of your day, reducing its overall grip.
